item.title: PHP2Shell is a warning shot for vulnerability disclosure
item.description: The technical details of web server stacks are worth learning about. Preferably not from the TV news. Last week, knowing about PHP was a niche professional interest. This week, cab drivers have opinions. PHP is not the story; it's the illustration. There are good reasons that it has this most unfortunate of spotlights . It's very old, and it shows. Growing from roots in the mid-1990s, it has never suffered from the straitjacket of a specification, and while it has seen a lot of refactoring and modernization, it retains design elements from more than 20 years ago. PHP is emphatically not the only project where urgent demands for better performance, reliability, and features consume the resources needed to tidy up ugly internals that appear to work just fine. Until, one day, that technical debt falls due. There will be many more days like this. PHP's significance is that it isn't unique. The details don't matter that much, although this annotated comic book version is both fun and granular if you want to learn about it. Now the dynamics of AI-assisted cybersecurity are becoming clearer, defenders can use the tools to uncover dangerous flaws, but motivated and inventive attackers can use them too. Neither side has a monopoly on resources or ingenuity. The pace and scale of the conflict are growing so quickly that we have to look at how actual global warfare works to reconfigure. The most pertinent aspect of PHP2Shell is the people, not the machines. We know how the LLMs identified the mix of problems and their exploitation over a few days in August, and we know how quickly any public information about such things can be weaponized. It took days, not months, to find, and hours rather than days to exploit. The correct protocol is to disclose patches privately to major, trusted organizations, and then when core services are protected, go public and go hard. But PHP2Shell didn't work out like that, because it was too tasty a treat to keep secret. The first attacks were seen days before the anonymous Hacker News post that announced the presence and severity of the problems. That post had the correct CVE numbers. It came from someone in the loop. The devastating effect of leaked intelligence and the tensions between keeping valuable data secret and being able to use it were abundantly apparent in the Second World War. This led to the system of clearances, classification, and trained liaison officers by which the output of places like Bletchley Park could be filtered, guided, and protected on its way to the people who needed it, and kept away from the eyeballs of those who didn't. It wasn't perfect, and security researchers don't need to work in huts while pretending to be supply clerks, but the lessons learned have proved good to this day. Disclosure needs to be a discipline, not a protocol. It's no good telling an entire IT sec team ahead of time – the absolute minimum number of people should hold the secret for as long as possible. The main value proposition is “ convenience living ”. Lagos has no shortage of ambitious residential developments. Across Victoria Island, Ikoyi and the Lekki corridor, new towers continue to reshape the city’s skyline, competing for the attention of homeowners and investors. Yet, as the premium property market becomes increasingly competitive, the question for developers is no longer simply how high they can build but what lasting value they can offer beyond the apartment itself. For Landmark Africa, the answer lies in a business model it has spent nearly three decades developing. With Landmark Waterview Apartments, the company is bringing residential ownership into one of Lagos’ most established business, leisure, and lifestyle destinations, combining contemporary homes with the commercial activity, hospitality infrastructure, and recreational experiences that have become synonymous with the Landmark brand. The 20-storey development, situated within Landmark Lagos ecosystem in Victoria Island, has apartments overlooking the Atlantic coastline and Lagos skyline. Approximately 40% of the apartments have already been sold, reflecting early market interest in a project that seeks to offer more than conventional apartment ownership. From Commercial Real Estate to Destination Development Landmark Africa’s journey began in 1997 with serviced offices, long before the concept of integrated lifestyle destinations became a prominent feature of Nigeria’s real estate market. Over the years, the company expanded into commercial property, mixed-use developments featuring hospitality, tourism, entertainment, and leisure components, developing a portfolio that reflects an increasingly diversified approach to real estate. Its flagship Landmark Lagos destination became one of the most visible expressions of that strategy. By bringing together corporate offices, event facilities, restaurants, hospitality, retail, andrecreational attractions, the company helped establish a destination that attracted more than four million visitors annually at its peak. The significance of that achievement extends beyond visitor numbers. It demonstrated Landmark’s ability to create and sustain commercial activity by attracting businesses and consumers to a shared destination. Waterview represents an important next step in that evolution: introducing residential ownership into an environment that has already established its commercial and lifestyle appeal. For buyers, this means investing in a property connected to an existing destination rather than relying solely on the promise of future neighbourhood development. item.title: PHP2Shell: No login, no app code, no warning. What next?
item.description: If you run PHP anywhere in your environment, patch to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 now. Two critical flaws disclosed last week, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed "PHP2Shell"), let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server with nothing more than a crafted web request. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, every earlier release is affected, and exploitation in the wild has been reported. The patch is the easy part. The hard part is finding every copy of PHP you own, because PHP rarely shows up where you expect it. This post covers what the flaws are, how far exploitation has gone, and how to get to full coverage fast. What happened Details leaked before the planned embargo, so the PHP security team moved fast and shipped fixes within about a day of announcing them. The two vulnerabilities Both bugs live in PHP core, not in any framework or plugin, so they reach anything that runs PHP to serve web requests. Affected server setups include PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP rates mod_php as the highest risk. No login is needed: the attacker only has to reach a PHP endpoint over HTTP. Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Every earlier release is affected. PHP has also published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, but there are no official releases for those branches. Treat a backport as a stopgap and plan the upgrade. Is it being exploited? Yes, though reliable public exploits are still scarce. watchTowr reports exploitation in its honeypot network as of October 21, and Tenable relays Cloudflare's CTO saying Cloudflare is seeing early attacks. Other telemetry, such as Patchstack's, shows mostly probing so far. Neither CVE is in CISA's KEV catalog yet, and no public indicators of compromise have been released. How hard the bug is to weaponize depends on the platform. VulnCheck reproduced both flaws and found: Code execution works on ARM64, and on x86 systems where address space layout randomization (ASLR) is turned off. Dozens of public proof-of-concepts exist, but very few work and none bypass ASLR on x86-64. Red Hat likewise rates RCE as hard in practice on default PHP-FPM deployments. Don't read that as permission to wait. Exploits mature quickly once a patch diff is public, and fake PoC repositories for headline CVEs often carry malware, so treat any you find with caution. Tanium's research on exploitability is in Why PHP2Shell is real(opens in a new tab). Most at risk: internet-facing PHP applications, especially those running mod_php or on ARM64 hosts. It's also worth retro-hunting recent web server and PHP-FPM logs for unexplained worker crashes and unusual multipart requests. Why finding PHP is harder than it looks No one has a complete list of PHP-based applications, and anything custom-built won't be on any list. PHP hides in several places at once: OS packages on Linux (php, php-fpm, php8.x), which package managers and most inventory tools see. Homebrew and similar on m

item.title: 'Let's just shove a bigger fan in there and see what happens'
item.description: IT people are asked to cram a lot into a working week, which is why The Register tries to ease readers into Monday with a new instalment of “Who, Me?” – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of office mistakes and escapes. This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as "Robert," who told us he worked for an outfit that scours newspapers and websites to find stories mentioning their clients. "We found key words in articles that customers were paying us to monitor for. We would then cut out the articles and send them to the customer," Robert explained. Sadly, business wasn't great. By the time Robert left it was almost bankrupt, and he gathers a fire sale ensued. That strained financial situation meant the company was very keen on keeping legacy hardware alive. "We had this one 2U pizza box server, and one of the three internal fans wore out," Robert explained. The server was so old no replacement was available. "So, we took the lid off and put a bigger fan on top of the component that needed the airflow," Robert confessed. The server couldn't tell the difference and kept working. Six months later, another internal fan broke. "The logical thing to do was to put another ill-fitted fan in/on the server to ensure that the airflow was good," Robert said. Again, the server didn’t have a problem with that. The server, which was an integral part of the company’s daily operations, was now operating with one original fan, no lid, and two non-standard fans precariously balanced over its exposed components. This rig mostly worked. "We had to be careful when working near the server, because too much shaking would cause the fans to fall over," Robert confessed. When the third internal fan died, management finally decided to buy a new box. Have you rigged risky hardware and gotten away with it? If so, share your story by clicking here to send email to Who, Me? We're pretty sure The Register's hardware will hold together long enough for us to tell your tale on some future Monday. ®

item.title: Tesco replacing VMware with Proxmox in its stores and on the edge
item.description: UK retail giant Tesco appears to have decided to replace VMware with Proxmox in its stores. A job ad for a new Head of Software Engineering: Edge Platform role says the gig involves leading “two major, interconnected engineering priorities: modernising Tesco’s edge virtualisation estate through the migration from VMware to Proxmox, and building a robust, scalable software-driven Edge Management Platform to provision, manage, monitor and maintain the retail edge estate throughout its lifecycle.” The stakes are high because the job ad says Tesco’s Edge Platform “provides the underlying computing environment and software capabilities that enable applications to run across our stores.” “Store technology must remain dependable despite connectivity disruptions, constrained local resources and the complexity of managing software and infrastructure changes across thousands of locations. Failures or poorly executed changes can directly affect store operations, colleague productivity and customer experience.” Whoever scores the job will “own the engineering strategy and execution of Tesco’s migration from VMware to Proxmox across the edge estate, delivering a secure, reliable and cost-effective alternative virtualisation platform” - and do it from Bengaluru, India. One KPI is “Safe and predictable migration from VMware to Proxmox, successful validation of required store configurations, reduced legacy dependencies and effective operational handover.” In case you came in late, Proxmox is an open-source virtualization platform offered by an Austrian company. The product has gained considerable interest as a VMware alternative for edge, hyperconverged, and basic server virtualization scenarios. Proxmox is trying to grow into a full software-defined datacenter contender, too. Independent analyst Michael Warrilow rates [PDF] Proxmox as technically strong but warns would-be users will need to find a support partner because until recently the company only offered support during business hours in Austria. That changed in September when Proxmox announced 24/7 support for enterprise customers. In an email to The Register , Warrilow said “Modernisation is the key to reducing the dependence on VMware: reduce legacy whilst adding incremental value to a new initiative.” “Supermarkets and general merchandise are ripe for this, more so given they are a location where VMware had more competition and less differentiation.” “The Tesco job spec has many of the ingredients for a next-gen, cloud-inspired instore experience,” he added. “API-driven, ‘programmable’ infrastructure that allows rapid deployment and a better experience for customers.” Tesco operates over 5,000 stores around the world. We’ve asked the retail giant to enumerate the extent of its planned Proxmox rollout. Scuttlebutt suggests Tesco will adopt Microsoft’s Hyper-V for its core workloads. item.title: Work to protect DNS from quantum decryption attacks is speeding up
item.description: Internet governance bodies are likely to accelerate work to prepare the domain name system (DNS) so it can remain secure once quantum computers can challenge conventional encryption. John Crain, ICANN’s chief technology officer, last week told The Register that he is aware of efforts within the organization, and at other internet governance bodies, to consider what happens once commercially available quantum computers become capable of easily deciphering encrypted information. Those machines theoretically pose a risk to DNSSEC, the Domain Name System Security Extensions that adapt PKI to the job of verifying the veracity of DNS records. The CTO said he’s aware of predictions that such computers could come online “at the turn of the decade” and that he has therefore changed his view of when the DNS needs to be made quantum safe. “If you asked me years ago, I would have said we probably need to be ready in ten years,” Crain said. “Now, maybe it's less than that. I don't know if it's three years or five, but it's probably not ten”. One way to quantum-proof DNSSEC is to use larger keys that even a quantum computer will struggle to crack. Doing so, however, runs into message size limits in the DNS. “If we go for larger key sizes, that means larger zones, larger packets, larger responses,” Crain said. It can also mean traffic being carried by multiple TCP packets, instead of the single UDP messages DNS prefers. Crain said ICANN, the IETF, and other internet governance bodies are aware of this challenge and have begun preliminary work to address it. “Being prepared to go from UDP to TCP is going to take a few years,” he told The Register at ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali last week. “We're probably a few years away from being able to deploy in a predictable manner.” The internet community has, however, seen that the problem is becoming more acute. “We're going to ramp up the speed of development,” Crain said. Internet registry reform nears At ICANN’s Bali conference, The Register also met Jia-Rong Low, in his capacity as chair of the Number Resource Organization, the peak body for the world’s five regional internet registries (RIRs), AFRINIC, APNIC, ARIN, LACNIC, and RIPE NCC. The topic of that conversation was Internet Coordination Policy 2 (ICP-2), the document that governs RIRs. In its current form, ICP-2 describes the formation of a new RIR but no other part of its operations. After strife at AFRINIC raised the possibility of the African registry failing, the NRO decided to update ICP-2 so it covered the entire lifecycle of an RIR, from formation through to possible derecognition. Work on ICP-2 has moved through several rounds of public consultation. It has reached the status of a recommended draft. Low told The Register work on the document has proven “very challenging” to develop entirely with remote work. Last week’s ICANN meeting, he said, offered a venue for in-person collaboration that he hopes will result in work accelerating. The revised docu

item.title: After threatening AI export bans, China allows DeepSeek to keep selling
item.description: China has proposed to restrict export of some AI technologies but quickly moved to allow some of its champion companies to continue shipping their wares abroad. Beijing’s Ministry of Commerce announced the restrictions in mid-October by revising its Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export in China. The restrictions mean that Chinese companies must apply for a license to export their tech. New entrants on the list included “23 technologies related to large-scale models, intelligent agents, computing clusters, and information processing.” Tech issued under open source licenses is exempt from the restrictions. Last Friday, Chinese state media reported that two companies – named elsewhere as DeepSeek and MiniMax – received authorization to continue exports. Both companies are credible challengers to American AI vendors, so letting them sell their wares abroad meets China’s goals of creating export industries and enhancing its tech sector. The expanded Catalogue also gives Beijing the ability to stop exports of any AI it feels represents important sovereign capacity, such as tools that are potent bug-finders or have military uses. China is not alone in restricting exports of AI technology: the USA has imposed on-again, off-again, bans on sales of advanced GPUs to China. AI datacenter bubble wobbles in Australia If the AI datacenter building bubble bursts, two recent Australian incidents may prove instructive. The first took place on October 9, when a company called Firmus called off its initial public offering. Firmus already operates four datacenters, two in Australia and a pair in Singapore. It plans several more, plus expansions of its existing bit barns. Meta has committed to spend over $700 million with the company. Private investors had already ploughed over $2 billion into the company. The float would have been Australia’s largest for 20 years and aimed to raise around $5 billion, giving Firmus a valuation over $40 billion. In the days before the float, investor sentiment suddenly soured. Would-be buyers reportedly asked Firmus to lower its share price and therefore valuation by perhaps a quarter, as they feared the company’s prospectus made very optimistic revenue predictions. Not helping matters was that one of Firmus’ founders did time after being convicted of insider trading. The company eventually cancelled its IPO. The other incident took place on Wednesday, when established datacenter operator NEXTDC announced [PDF] reduced revenue forecasts because its chosen power supplier suspended work “because of community and stakeholder opposition.” That opposition related to installation of poles and wires needed to bring juice to an existing datacenter NEXTDC intends to expand. Protestors have blocked access to the site, and the local council has decided not to allow the power company to use relevant roads while community consultation continues. item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
item.description: null On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen. When it reappeared on the west side again, Cassini realized that Iapetus must be darker on one side than the other , which made it harder to see when the dark side was facing Earth. More than 300 years later, NASA sent a spacecraft named Cassini to Saturn, and that Cassini took some pretty awesome photos of Iapetus. Realizing Iapetus kind of resembled a yin-yang, it has since been nicknamed the " yin-yang moon ." This image taken by the Cassini spacecraft shows what the two-tone surface of the moon Iapetus looks like without false color. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute) How it mattered The discovery of Iapetus, with its yin-yang bright and dark hemispheres, has added to our understanding of how moons form. "Using the computer simulations, the researchers concluded ... the inner moons of Saturn and its gorgeous rings are all relatively young. The more distant moons Titan and Iapetus would not have been formed at the same time." "Our best guess is that Saturn had a similar collection of moons before, but their orbits were disturbed by a special kind of orbital resonance involving Saturn's motion around the sun. Eventually, the orbits of neighboring moons crossed, and these objects collided. From this rubble, the present set of moons and rings formed." Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Want to build a UK datacenter? Please hold while Whitehall transfers you
item.description: Building a UK datacenter spans three government departments: one handles datacenter policy, another telecoms, and a third energy. MPs this week explored what Prime Minister Andy Burnham's summer reshuffle means for businesses navigating Whitehall. Liz Lloyd, parliamentary under-secretary of state, sits across two departments with a portfolio of responsibilities as long as a weekly shopping list. She explained to MPs this week that, following the decision to get rid of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), liaison with the tech industry on datacenter construction fell to the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST). Lloyd, who works across BIST and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), went on to explain that digital infrastructure sits within DCMS. Speaking to the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee, Lloyd acknowledged that some departmental responsibilities overlapped. "In terms of sector responsibilities, that is clear that technology, sorry, that telecom sits with DCMS and datacenters with BIST. When you're actually in an industry or you're trying to run a business, that that that is clear," the junior minister said. Any business trying to build a datacenter might also want to know how to get power to it. As far as The Register can figure out, that would be the Department for Energy and Net Zero. Planning permission rests with local government, although the overall policy lies with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. It may be clear, but it is hardly simple. The problem is real, though. Earlier this month, Microsoft pulled out of plans for Britain's largest AI supercomputer because of difficulties securing power for the facility. Elsewhere in the hearing, Lloyd was asked about the government's early 2025 claim that modernizing aging technology and digitizing processes could deliver £45 billion in productivity savings. Asked if the government stood by the figure, the junior minister said: "The £45 billion figure was an estimate of long-term productivity gains. It wasn't a kind of one-off figure for savings… it was never a figure that was a target or a cashable savings figure." When the figure was publicized under the Starmer government in January 2025, the press release was headed "Archaic tech sees public sector miss £45 billion annual savings." It continued: "Taxpayer funded services from the NHS to local councils are missing out on £45 billion in productivity savings because they are too often dependent on old and outdated technology." It claimed the government would "tackle these issues" using "digital tools, AI and common sense to overhaul public sector technology." ®

item.title: October's 'Hunter's Moon' stalks into the autumn sky tonight: Here's what you need to know
item.description: null October's full "Hunter's Moon" treated stargazers to a mesmerizing natural light show when it rose overnight on Oct. 25-26! Check out our wrap article to see the best photos of the October full moon . The October full moon rises tonight! Here's everything you need to know about the "Hunter's Moon," including where to see it, how it got its name and other tricks of the light and mind that could conspire to create a truly spectacular lunar light show. October's moon reaches 100% illumination at 12:12 a.m. EDT (0412 GMT) on Oct. 26, as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. The shadowy terminator that separates the day and night side of the moon is conspicuously absent around this time, as are the shadows that throw craters into spectacular relief during the waxing and waning lunar phases. Instead, it's a perfect time to explore the dark lunar "seas" that cover the moon's surface where lava flooded impact basins billions of years ago, before hardening to create enormous basaltic plains. Streaks of reflective material can also be spotted streaking away from bright young craters, where material from the lunar subsurface was excavated and cast across the moon's surface during brutal asteroid impacts. Where and when to see the October full moon. Stargazers in the U.S. will get their first view of the full moon as it climbs into the eastern sky at sunset on Oct. 25. Be sure to check out Time and Date's moonrise tracker to discover the exact timings for your location. The moon often appears particularly large while close to the horizon, thanks to a phenomenon called the "Moon Effect," wherein our brains trick us into thinking that the lunar disk is larger while in close visual proximity to the ground than it is when overhead. The moon can also take on a spectacular yellow-orange color in the hour after moonrise, as blue wavelengths of its reflected light — the shortest in the visible spectrum — are scattered during its oblique passage through Earth's atmosphere . Why is the October full moon called the "Hunter's Moon"? October's full moon is commonly known as the Hunter's Moon in the Northern Hemisphere because it rises soon after farmers have cleared away the summer's harvest, leaving the fields bare for hunters to catch their prey and prepare it as food for the winter, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . It's also called the "Migrating Moon" by the North American Cree people, in reference to the birds that travel to warmer climates around the time of its rising. The Ojibwe and the Haida know it asthe "Freezing Moon," to reflect the drop in temperature that occurs in autumn. Want to make the most of the October full moon? Then be sure to check out our guide to observing the moon and photographing the lunar disk , along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography . item.title: Veekee James’ Sheer Beaded Bodice Leads Wine-Red Fashion at Zlatan Ibile’s Wedding | See Photos
item.description: Veekee James showcasing her custom wine-red corset dress and gold woven box clutch. Veekee James at a party? Trust her to come dressed like the celebration has its own red carpet. And when it’s a Nigerian wedding, with good music, beautiful traditional outfits and guests who take their fashion very seriously, you already know she’s going to have some fun with her look. Yesterday, Afrobeats star Zlatan Ibile , whose real name is Omoniyi Temidayo Raphael , and his partner, Davita Omoniyi , celebrated their traditional wedding with family, friends and some familiar faces from the entertainment industry. Among the guests was Nigerian fashion designer Veekee James, who arrived in a gorgeous wine-red and champagne creation from her own fashion label. And between the sculpted corset, the beaded sleeves and that towering gele, there was so much to admire. Veekee James in a custom wine-red sheer corset dress with metallic sequin detailing and a structured metallic gele. Let’s start with the dress. Veekee chose a floor-length, figure-hugging design featuring a sheer corset-style bodice covered in vertical rows of wine-red crystals. The sweetheart-inspired neckline extended into a high, embellished collar, while the long sheer sleeves featured rows of burgundy beads. The fitted skirt followed a mermaid silhouette, with sweeping patterns of gold sequins, wine-red embroidery and dusty-rose detailing running down to a subtle train. Structural details of the sheer corset bodice, crystal neckband, and sequin wave skirt on Veekee James’ wedding guest dress. And that gele! Veekee went for a tall, fan-pleated design in metallic champagne, giving her look even more height and making the headwrap a fashion moment of its own. She paired it with burgundy drop earrings, a structured gold woven box clutch and soft, neutral makeup that complemented the colours of her outfit. Styling details of Veekee James’ high-neck crystal collar, sheer corset bodice, and pleated metallic gele. Of course, Veekee knows her way around a corset. As the founder and creative director of her eponymous fashion label, she’s known for sculpted silhouettes, detailed beadwork and glamorous occasionwear. For Zlatan and Davita’s wedding, she brought those design elements into her own wardrobe, pairing a fitted, heavily embellished dress with a traditional gele. What we particularly love is how the colours work together. The deep wine-red gives the dress its richness, while the champagne and gold details brighten the overall look. Even with the crystals, beading and high neckline, the accessories have their place, from the matching earrings to the gold clutch. Veekee James posing alongside her husband Femi Atere at Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi’s wedding. And if you’ve been looking for wedding guest inspiration, Veekee’s outfit offers a lovely styling idea: when your dress has this much detail around the neckline, you can leave out the necklace and let your earrings and gele do their thing. item.description: Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi celebrating their Yoruba cultural heritage during their wedding ceremony. Lemon yellow and mint green? Now that’s a colour combination we can get behind. For their second traditional wedding look, Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi ( Omoniyi Temidayo Raphael ) have switched things up, trading their earlier burgundy and ivory outfits for a softer palette that feels right at home at a Yoruba wedding. And if you thought one outfit change was enough for this celebration, you know Nigerian weddings better than that! Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi in custom Mazelle Bridal pastel Yoruba traditional attire, styled by Goodnews Emmanuel Icon. After honouring Davita’s Edo heritage in their first look, the couple are now celebrating Zlatan’s Yoruba roots in coordinated outfits by Mazelle Bridal. Davita wears a custom lemon-yellow gown with a sculpted, corset-style bodice, a sweetheart-inspired neckline and long sleeves with flared cuffs. Mint-green appliqué forms swirling, floral-inspired patterns across the bodice and fitted, floor-length skirt, with gold-toned accents adding extra detail. Davita Omoniyi showcasing her custom Mazelle Bridal outfit for her Yoruba traditional wedding look. She completes the look with a large, pleated lemon-yellow gele and matching sheer fabric draped over her arm. A green statement necklace, matching earrings and a mint-green clutch bring the accessories together, while the soft yellow and green palette gives her bridal look a fresh, coordinated finish. Davita Omoniyi wearing a pleated circular gele and sheer veil for her second traditional wedding outfit change. Zlatan matches her in a custom mint-green agbada by Mazelle Bridal, featuring subtle embroidery across the chest. He finishes his outfit with a structured fila, layers of white beads and a carved green walking stick that picks up the colour of his attire. Zlatan Ibile in a custom Mazelle Bridal Agbada set for his Yoruba traditional wedding. Styled by Goodnews Emmanuel Icon, the couple pose hand in hand against a plum backdrop. Their first look celebrated Davita’s Edo heritage, and this second outfit honours Zlatan’s Yoruba roots, giving their wedding wardrobe two lovely cultural chapters. And with lemon yellow and mint green taking centre stage, this outfit change has given us another reason to keep up with their wedding style. item.title: How AI Can Expand Opportunities for African Youth – Discussions to Expect at Goalkeepers 2026 Dakar
item.description: AI could be a great equaliser, but only if it’s built intentionally to benefit the people who need it most. Credit: Gates Foundation . During the 2026 ADF-YGL Convening in Lagos , young leaders from across the world, including Africa, gathered at Learn2Earn Academy, an AI talent factory founded by Iyinoluwa Aboyeji . There, the global leaders were introduced to a few students who have been using AI to build solutions for some of the day-to-day challenges that Africans, Nigerians specifically, face. One of them was Anas Masama, who showcased ‘Morrow’, a fintech app that allows offline transfers without internet connectivity. Anas explained that despite the wide coverage of internet providers in Nigeria, the internet’s strength fluctuates or sometimes goes offline and leaves Nigerians stranded at a point of payment. With AI, he built ‘Morrow’ to solve two problems: 1) The embarrassment that a Nigerian might feel due to bad internet connectivity. 2) Time. Anas’ invention is an example of the potential opportunities that exist when Africans leverage AI to solve basic issues. While there are concerns about the risks of AI use in Africa, including hallucinations, stereotypical results and many others, it remains one of the fastest-growing technological advancements in recent times. AI continues to grow and become more efficient, and the most urgent task Africans can embark on is to upskill in how to adopt AI for better use, so the continent doesn’t get left behind. In the 2026 Goalkeepers Report , Bill Gates calls for three actions now that will help AI improve lives and livelihoods for more people in the years ahead: Make AI tools work in every language people speak; ground AI tools in local data; and invest in people and access in the places and populations they are intended to serve. All three suggestions apply to Africa so it can properly leverage AI to expand opportunities. At present, despite how expansive AI has become, it is built in places far away from Africa. This is why Africans, who have access to local data and speak African languages, should build AI tools that incorporate local data and African languages for better use. This way, AI has access to specific data of Africans and will allow it to better understand cultural contexts and pragmatics. This will make a great equaliser rather than make things less equal. Of course, Africans still encounter basic challenges like electricity, connectivity, access to phones, and other issues, but those who have access must maximise it greatly to help others. This year’s Goalkeepers 2026 is centred around this conversation. After hosting engaging and immersive events in the Nordics and New York, Goalkeepers is coming to Dakar on October 29. This event, “Equitable AI and the Future of African Youth”, aims to discuss how AI can create opportunities for Africans across various sectors while also addressing the challenges the continent faces. item.title: Davido, Zlatan & Shoday Turn Their “Nakupenda” Performance Into a London Sing-Along
item.description: Shoday, Zlatan Ibile, and Davido performing Nakupenda live on stage during their London concert setup. Photo Credit: Davido/Instagram “Oh my God, what is this? (What is what?)” You already know what comes next. We’re taking you straight to London, where Davido , Zlatan and Shoday had an entire arena singing along to “ Nakupenda ”. And judging by the crowd, nobody needed convincing to join in. Phones were up, voices were loud, and thousands of fans were enjoying every moment of the performance. There’s something so lovely about watching a song travel from our speakers to a stage thousands of miles away, with a crowd singing every word right back to the artistes. That’s exactly what happened when Davido and Zlatan performed “Nakupenda” alongside Shoday, giving the London audience a performance filled with music, dancing and some very happy fans. Davido took to the stage in a white tank top and green trousers, moving across the platform as the audience sang along. Zlatan joined him in a tactical vest and red trousers, bringing his familiar dance moves into the mix. With dancers adding to the performance and the crowd responding to every verse, there was hardly a moment when the arena wasn’t buzzing. And can we talk about those phone flashlights? Seeing thousands of them raised across the arena while everyone sang together was such a beautiful sight. It’s one thing to enjoy “Nakupenda” through your headphones, but hearing an entire crowd sing it back to Davido, Zlatan and Shoday is a whole different experience. item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
item.description: null On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film. When they saw the images for the first time, the scientists were literally jumping up and down with joy. This photo is the first view of Earth from space taken by a camera on a U.S. Army V-2 rocket launched from White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico on Oct. 24, 1946. (Image credit: U.S. Army) How it mattered The ability to photograph Earth from space drove both an expanded interest to continue pushing into space and led to unexpected societal changes with regards to how humanity considered its home planet. For military and intelligence agencies, the potential now existed for reconnaissance at a far larger scale than what was possible with high-altitude aircraft. That capability expanded to agriculture and meteorological purposes, eventually making Earth observation one of the most common reasons satellites and space stations are deployed into orbit today. Earth photography from space also gave birth to the environmental movement, as people began to see the planet differently. The fragility of this orb became more apparent, as now Earth appeared a "blue marble" set against an endless black void. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Milan Meets Lagos: Salone del Mobile Makes a Stunning Debut at Design Week Lagos 2026!
item.description: The global design world just got a major dose of Lagos energy! In a historic moment for the African creative scene, the world-renowned Salone del Mobile . Milano officially touched down in Nigeria for the very first time during Design Week Lagos 2026. Held at the iconic National Theatre, the high-profile gathering brought together international design heavyweights, top Nigerian architects, interior designers, business leaders, and cultural icons for an unforgettable exchange of ideas and inspiration. Leading the Italian delegation were Marco Sabetta , General Manager, Salone del Mobile and the legendary Marva Griffin Wilshire, Founder & Curator, SaloneSatellite. The strategic visit highlights Nigeria’s booming demand for luxury design and luxury living, with demand for Italian craftsmanship reaching record highs across the continent. Honors & Cultural Magic A major highlight of the week was the inaugural IDEA Honours, where Marva Griffin Wilshire received the Architectural Legacy Honour—complete with a breathtaking custom award plaque crafted by iconic Nigerian master Demas Nwoko , MFR. Also celebrated were visionary architect Lesley Lokko and celebrated artist Yinka Shonibare CBE. “Being here in Lagos today allowed us to discover remarkable new African talent and build the conditions that will help young designers forge their paths globally, ” shared an inspired Marva Griffin Wilshire. Making a New Africa From guided exhibition tours to rich panel sessions focused on this year’s theme, Making a New Africa: From Material to Market, the atmosphere was charged with ambition and creativity. Design Week Lagos founder Titi Ogufer e emphasized that Africa’s rich materials, heritage, and creative talent are ready to drive global industrial growth. With Design Week Lagos running through October 25th, the city has firmly cemented its status as Africa’s ultimate capital for design, innovation, and style. Next stop? Milan for the 65th edition of Salone del Mobile in April 2027! item.title: A Royal Love Story! Zlatan Ibile & Davita Omoniyi’s Edo Traditional Wedding Looks
item.description: Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi holding hands during their Edo traditional wedding, styled by Goodnews Emmanuel Icon. What a beautiful day for love! Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi are celebrating their traditional wedding today, and we’re starting the day with their beautiful first look. The Afrobeats star and his bride-to-be have chosen to honour Davita’s Edo heritage with coordinated traditional wedding attire, from her richly embellished burgundy gown to his regal ivory outfit. And there’s so much to love about the details. For their first appearance, Zlatan, whose real name is Omoniyi Temidayo Raphael , and Davita chose to honour her Edo heritage. And what better way to celebrate love than by showing up in outfits that tell a beautiful story about where you come from? Zlatan Ibile kissing Davita Omoniyi’s hand in their custom Edo cultural attire, styled by Goodnews Emmanuel Icon. Davita looked every inch the Edo bride in a custom burgundy gown by Dova Bridals. The corseted mermaid design featured a curved sweetheart neckline, sheer long sleeves and a sweeping side train. Red crystal beads formed beautiful lattice patterns across the gown, while her traditional Okuku braided crown and layers of coral necklaces completed the look. She also carried a black horsehair fly whisk, with a sheer crimson veil draped over her crown. Davita Omoniyi as an Edo bride seated on a carved throne in a custom Dova Bridals gown. And Zlatan? The groom was every bit as regal beside his bride. He wore a custom cream robe by Deji & Kola, topped with a textured ivory coat featuring hand-stitched red beadwork along the shoulders and hem. The red details tied his outfit beautifully to Davita’s, while layers of coral beads, an ivory ceremonial cap and a carved wooden staff completed his traditional look. Zlatan Ibile wearing a custom Deji & Kola cream robe and layered coral beads for his traditional wedding. Styled by Goodnews Emmanuel Icon, the couple posed against a warm ombré backdrop, with Zlatan seated on a carved gold throne beneath a tasseled umbrella. Between the coordinated outfits, the traditional accessories and the beautiful celebration of Davita’s Edo roots, their first wedding look is one we’ll be admiring for a while. item.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
item.description:
Matthew has more than 30 years of experience talking about movies, TV shows, and video games, and for 20 of those years someone has actually paid him to do it. He's just as surprised as you are.

He has a degree in Film from Vassar College and a degree in gaming from growing up in the '80s and '90s. He has written for both print and online outlets, including The Escapist, MTV, Flixist, Destructoid, Variety, and the Washington Post.

He will still gladly talk anyone's ear off about Marvel, Star Wars, Doctor Who, Zelda, and Star Trek.

It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie. "Star Trek" — a show built on progressive ideals, thoughtful characters, and boundary-breaking television — was completely and totally afraid to say anything at all. Mash it up, Scotty (Image credit: Paramount) To be clear, "Star Trek" is no stranger to genre mashups, and they're not inherently a bad thing. Trek has been running for nearly 1,000 total episodes, and they've been doing mashups since the very first season of "Star Trek: The Original Series", which featured gangster, historical fiction, and war-themed episodes. The holodeck took things further, giving the writers an excuse to set the action anywhere they could dream up. No more alien planets that look suspiciously like Earth were necessary to completely flip the series’ genre; just work up a hologram malfunction and suddenly "Trek" is a Sherlock Holmes-esque mystery or a noir thriller. And even without the holodeck, genres are fluid things that often take from each other to tell stories within each other’s realms. But while "Trek" has always dabbled, it's never done an entire season of genre episodes… in fact, that might be unprecedented in all of science fiction TV itself, let alone "Star Trek". This season of "SNW" didn’t use occasional gimmicks to take a break from space fare; it was all gimmick, all the time. Check out the episode rundown below: Episode 1: Dinosaur adventure/western (Land of the Lost) Episode 2: Space horror (Event Horizon) Episode 3: Raunchy comedy (The Hangover) Episode 4: Wartime drama (Casablanca)* Episode 5: Puppets (The Muppets) Episode 6: Disaster movie/real-time story (The Poseidon Adventure) Episode 7: Soap opera (Days of Our Lives) Episode 8: Cold War film/submarine movie (The Hunt for Red October) Episod

item.title: Medusa's eye, Halloween fireballs and more: 5 skywatching targets to look out for this spooky season
item.description: null The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore. Ancient Celtic druids would hold the celebration of Samhain — the precursor to Halloween — when the star cluster reached its highest point in the autumn night sky at midnight . The Pleiades open star cluster glows in the blackness of space. (Image credit: Photo by Lorenzo Di Cola/NurPhoto via Getty Images) The veil separating the worlds of the living and the dead was believed to be at its thinnest around this time, granting the departed a brief window to visit the living before the realms separated once again. The Pleiades appears as a tight collection of six or seven bright twinkling stars to the naked eye, while a pair of binoculars will reveal dozens more of the 1,000-strong star cluster. How to find the Pleiades in October using Orion's Belt. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Stargazers in the U.S. can find the Pleiades using the three familiar stars of Orion's Belt , which glisten in the eastern sky in the hours preceding midnight. Trace an imaginary line upward through the trio of stars until you find the bright orange star Aldebaran, which represents an eye of the great bull represented in the constellation Taurus . The Pleiades can be found glowing less than 15 degrees above! (Reminder: Your clenched fist held at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky.) The 'Demon Star' Algol Next we turn our gaze to the "Demon Star" Algol — a beautiful binary system that represents an eye of the monstrous Gorgon Medusa, whose severed head is depicted in the constellation Perseus . The demon star Algol shines above the southeastern horizon after sunset in October. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) The demonic eye appears to "wink" at us every 2.867 days, as one of a pair of co-orbiting stars eclipses the other, making Algol appear 3.3 times dimmer than usual at the climax, or "minima," of each 10-hour eclipse. Algol won't be eclipsed on Halloween night in 2026, though you may notice its light dim during the surrounding minima on Oct. 29 and Nov. 1, according to Sky and Telescope . Cetus, the sea monster The night sky is often described as a sea of stars, so it's only fitting that a monster lurks within its depths. The constellation Cetus — also known as the sea monster, or the whale — can be found shining i

item.title: SpaceX launches Starlink satellites from California as Falcon 9 cadence slows (video)
item.description: null SpaceX launched its newest batch of Starlink broadband internet satellites today (Oct. 23) from the California coast. The spacecraft, Starlink Group 15-15, were stacked 27 high inside the payload fairing of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket , which lifted off from Pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base at 6:48 p.m. EDT (2248 GMT; 3:48 p.m. local time in California). The rocket's first stage booster, designated B1063, executed its main engine cutoff and stage separation about 2.5 minutes into flight, sending the second stage to continue onward to low Earth orbit (LEO). The vehicle's two-piece protective payload fairing was jettisoned just before T+3 minutes. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches 27 Starlink satellites from California on Oct. 23, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) The booster, meanwhile, reoriented for its descent back to Earth. As the mission clock passed 8 minutes, B1063 began its landing burn, and it touched down about 20 seconds later on SpaceX's droneship "Of Course I Still Love You." This was the 36th launch and landing for B1063, which notably launched NASA's DART asteroid-smashing mission in November 2021. The Falcon 9's upper stage completed its first engine burn shortly after B1063 landed and will coast for about 45 minutes before initiating a second and final orbital insertion burn. Following that burn's execution, deployment of the vehicle's 27 satellites into LEO is scheduled to begin 62 minutes after launch. The Falcon 9's first stage, shortly after its drone-ship landing on Oct. 23, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Previous Booster B1063 launches Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich | DART | Transporter-7 | Iridium OneWeb | SDA-0B | NROL-113 | NROL-167 | NROL-149 | NAOS | 26 Starlink missions Today's Starlink liftoff adds to SpaceX's growing constellation of more than 11,000 active spacecraft. But Starlinks aren't launching quite as often as they used to, as SpaceX shifts its focus from the Falcon 9 to its bigger and more powerful Starship rocket. Starship is designed for full reusability and is equipped with a payload bay outfitted to accommodate SpaceX's upgraded Version 3 Starlink satellites, which are too large for the workhorse Falcon 9. Starship is still under development, but once the rocket begins operational flights (and that day is getting closer), SpaceX plans to phase out the Falcon 9 and its Falcon Heavy variant almost entirely. Falcon 9's 100th launch of 2026 was the Starlink 10-49 group from SpaceX's pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, which was later revealed to be the final Falcon 9 Starlink mission that would fly from Florida's Space Coast. The same might soon be true for Starlink launches from the West Coast as well. The reduction in missions lifting off from Florida has slowed Falcon 9's Starlink launch cadence considerably. At their peak, these missions were flying every two to three days. But the most recent one before today lifted off 11 days ago , and that launch itself was the first Starlink mission in more than

item.title: NASA lays out plan for Artemis 3 moon-lander test flight —but when will it launch?
item.description: null NASA just gave us our best look yet at its Artemis III moon-lander test flight. The agency laid out a detailed concept of operations for Artemis III today (Oct. 23) during a press conference at Kennedy Space Center , stressing how important the flight is to its moon plans and how challenging it will be to make everything go right. "We're launching three of the most powerful rockets in the world, and undertaking what is likely the most complicated launch campaign ever undertaken," Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, said during today's event, which lasted more than two hours. The baseline concept of operations for NASA's Artemis III docking test in low Earth orbit. (Image credit: NASA) Those three rockets are NASA's Space Launch System (SLS), SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's New Glenn , all of which will fly from Florida's Space Coast. If all goes according to plan, New Glenn will lift off first, carrying Blue Origin's Blue Moon lunar lander to low Earth orbit (LEO). SLS will go next, launching the Artemis III astronauts — NASA's Randy Bresnik, Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio, and the European Space Agency's Luca Parmitano — aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft . SLS will deploy Orion into a highly elliptical orbit, one that gets as close to Earth as 18 miles (29 kilometers) and as far away as 1,122 miles (1,806 km), according to Parsons. The capsule will then maneuver itself into an orbit with an altitude of about 345 miles (555 km). "That's really about getting thermal stability," Parsons said. "Orion was built as a deep-space vehicle, and so we're going to have to really manage the thermal environments, which are higher in a low Earth orbit." The Artemis III crew will spend two days checking out Orion and its systems in LEO before meeting up with Blue Moon, which will take place on Flight Day 3 at an altitude of 273 miles (439 km). "Over the next two days, the crew will conduct operations docked with Blue Moon," Parsons said. "They're going to open up the hatch. They're going to enter the lander. They're going to evaluate the environmental controls, the life support systems. We'll confirm that the spacecraft can maintain the right atmospheric pressure, and we're also going to test emergency scenarios, dual vehicle control, and we're going to put our Mission Control teams through their paces." After those operations are complete — likely on Flight Day 6 or thereabouts — Starship will launch, with a specially built docking adapter on its nose. The SpaceX vehicle — the 171-foot-tall (52 meters) upper stage of its fully reusable Starship megarocket — will meet up with Orion in LEO on Flight Day 8, at an altitude of about 237 miles (381 km). But this will be a very different encounter than the rendezvous with Blue Moon. "The demonstration with Starship is shorter, about two hours," Parsons said. item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 23, 2007: NASA launches Harmony module to ISS on STS-120 space shuttle mission
item.description: null On October 23, 2007, the space shuttle Discovery launched the Harmony module to the International Space Station . The Harmony module is a utility hub 14 feet wide and 24 feet long, or about the length of a minibus. It joins the European Space Agency's Columbus module and Japan's Kibo laboratory and serves as the crew quarters for the American astronauts. Once it was installed, the space station grew from about the size of a three-bedroom house to something more like a five-bedroom house. When astronauts delivered Harmony to the space station , they left it temporarily attached to the Unity node. After the shuttle left, astronauts used the space station's robotic arm to move the shuttle docking port out of the way at the Destiny module. This made room for Harmony to then dock at its permanent home next to the Destiny module. The U.S. Harmony node flew to space aboard space shuttle Discovery during mission STS-120, in October 2007, to be a connecting module and allow a larger space station. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered In 2007, the International Space Station was much smaller than it is today in terms of living space for its astronaut crew. The Harmony connecting module changed all that. The STS-120 mission opened a new phase of ISS expansion by adding a vital connecting hub for future modules. Prior to Harmony's launch, the last new room addition to the ISS had occurred in 2001, when Russia's Pirs docking module (since discarded) arrived. The Harmony module ( its original name was Node 2 ), was the second NASA-led hub module (after the Unity, or Node 1, module) for the ISS. It was built for NASA by the Italy-based Thales Alenia Space and is covered with five "common berthing mechanisms," or connecting points for different ISS modules. After the two-week STS-120 flight, Harmony was moved from a temporary berth at the Unity module to the forward port on the NASA's main Destiny laboratory. Once there, it served as a connection point for Europe's Columbus lab on the starboard side, and Japan's massive Kibo lab on the port side. Some of its ports have been used by visiting caargo ships and a docking port on its roof allows visiting vehicles to park there. Inside the module are eight payload racks that include four used for avionics and four others for either stowage or crew quarters. NASA's astronaut crew quarters are based in the Harmony module. The name Harmony was selected durng a public naming contest by NASA. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Halley's Comet dazzles from afar in spectacular astrophoto of Orionid meteor shower
item.description: null Tim McCollum captured a stunning view of Orionid meteors in the early hours of Oct. 21. (Image credit: Tim McCollum) Astrophotographer Tim McCollum captured a spectacular view of Orionid meteors sharing the night sky with a host of deep sky wonders on Oct. 21, as the annual shooting star display ramped up to peak activity. Comet 1P/Halley may be over 3 billion miles (4.8 kilometers) from Earth , but that didn't stop it from putting on a breathtaking display earlier this week, as particles cast off by the ancient wanderer carved a fiery path through the autumn sky. McCollum was able to capture a trio of vivid Orionid meteors as they streaked through the night sky above the city of Toccoa, Georgia, between 3-4 a.m. on Oct. 21. Each of the shooting stars can be seen racing away from the shower's apparent point of origin — or radiant — which is located close to the red giant star Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion . Successfully imaging a shooting star takes a combination of skill, luck and patience. McCollum photographed the meteors over the course of multiple 30-second exposures taken with a Canon EOS Ra camera and RF 28-70 f2.0 lens, which was fixed unerringly on the radiant with the aid of a star tracker. The individual exposures were then combined into a single composite image using the astrophoto software PixInsight. Nebulas and star clusters shine alongside fast-moving Orionid meteors. (Image credit: Tim McCollum) Canon EOS R7 camera (Image credit: Future/Kimberley Lane) The Canon EOS R7 is the best camera for beginners. Despite its crop sensor, the EOS R7 can rival most full-frame cameras. It features a 34.4MP sensor, ISO range up to 32,000 and a video capability of 4K UHD 60p. It has the best tools to help a beginner master photography. Read our full Canon EOS R7 review. The familiar stars of Orion's Belt glisten to the right of McCollum's image, close to the glow of the Orion Nebula — one of the nearest major star forming regions to Earth. The Rosette Nebula (Caldwell 49) can also be spotted embedded in the dense starfield and dust lanes of the Milky Way's galactic plane, which runs diagonally through the composite image, as can numerous star clusters. The Orionid meteor shower is active until Nov. 7, so be sure to head outside over the next few nights for a chance to spot one of Comet 1P/Halley's dazzling shooting stars . If you're lucky, you may even spot a Halloween Fireball belonging to the Taurid meteor shower , as Earth passes through the debris streams cast off by Comet 2P/Encke! Why not read our handy guide to photographing shooting stars ? You can also take a look at our picks of the best lenses and cameras for astrophotography available in 2026, including the Canon EOS R8 , which delivers the essential interval shooting functionality you need to capture meteors without bursting the bank. item.title: Never finishing the fight: Where did Xbox go wrong with Halo?
item.description: Halo: Campaign Evolved was Xbox’s second attempt at refreshing the 2001 sci-fi FPS classic, and it is perfectly fine. A cromulent remake, if ever there was one, but it’s hardly a franchise-saver, especially as Xbox looks to rethink its studio structure and approach to renowned IPs like Halo or Gears of War . Halo hasn’t been the same since original developer Bungie — now owned by Sony and working on Destiny and Marathon — departed, leaving 343 Industries (now Halo Studios) to guide the franchise. Neither Halo 4 nor 5 meaningfully evolved the gameplay formula or overarching narrative. Halo Infinite found more success by reheating what “old Halo felt like” and sticking it into a half-baked open world, but it still felt far from the series’ glory days. This year’s full remake of Combat Evolved's campaign delivered exactly what it promised: a shiny, 2026 version of the game that made audiences fall in love with the franchise. It was a clear attempt to reignite faith in 343’s vision, but how is a faithful, shinier remake proof of anything? It might not even matter anymore, as the new Xbox leadership has rocked the ship again, leaving Master Chief and the universe’s future cloudier than ever before. Now, with rumors of a reboot being considered at new steward Activision, is there hope for the Spartans, or will Xbox run into another dead end? Rebooted or not, Halo needs to leave Master Chief behind (Image credit: Xbox Game Studios) It looks like the ‘Halo Studios’ moniker only lasted a single (remade) game, as Xbox has recently announced that Call of Duty maker and publisher Activision — which houses many FPS-oriented studios — is taking over development, essentially leaving the 343 veterans as a minor support studio, which translates into more layoffs . If we put aside the human and institutional cost of this whole back-and-forth over the years (a big ask in today’s climate), there are reasons to be optimistic about the quality of an Activision-developed Halo. Regardless of what you think about the Call of Duty IP in 2026 and the publisher’s overall vision for it, it’s clear there’s plenty of talent holding everything together and, more importantly, enough experience to iterate on what Halo’s multiplayer side needs to shine bright again. (Image credit: Xbox Game Studios) But this won’t fix the larger issue with Halo, which is that Master Chief should’ve been left behind long ago. Like it or not, it’s difficult to deny Halo’s “golden era” ended with Halo: Reach (Bungie’s swansong under Xbox) and the Halo Wars spinoffs, which took the series into the real-time strategy genre. These games were wildly different, but they had one core thing in common: they made the sci-fi setting feel bigger instead of smaller, offering the perfect blueprint to build upon in a post-Halo 3 world. There’s nothing inherently wrong with the Master Chief. Franchises can be built around iconic characters like Mario or Lara Croft. But in the post-Bungie era, his role c

item.title: A farewell to BioWare, maker of some of the best games of the 21st century | Lucy James
item.description: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series Earlier this week, EA announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history of compelling role-playing games, complex characters and bold, choice-driven narratives. Its forthcoming game in the Mass Effect sci-fi series has been cancelled, and more than 400 people are losing their jobs. As someone who has worked in the video games industry for 15 years and spent almost 20 as a BioWare fan, I am among millions of mourners today. It’s not terribly hard to see why BioWare got the chop. Its parent company has been saddled with $20bn of debt thanks to a recent leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and the Saudi wealth fund. EA was looking for weight to cut loose, and despite its hardcore fanbase and reputation for genre-defining RPGs such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, BioWare hadn’t put out a critical or commercial hit in over 10 years. Its forthcoming game, titled Mass Effect: Universe according to a leaked trailer , was announced back in 2020. Despite some flashy teases, it was still years away from release. Continue reading...

item.title: Private Griffin moon lander gets put to the test | Space photo of the day for Oct. 23, 2026
item.description: null The Griffin-1 lunar lander undergoes testing at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The robotic Griffin lunar lander has passed a host of critical tests ahead of its first-ever moon mission, which is scheduled to launch later this year. What is it? At NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, Voyager Technologies' Griffin Mission One (or Griffin-1 ) lunar lander has gone through an absolute gauntlet of tests. The spacecraft was put through environmental testing that explored how the vehicle will fare in the extreme conditions it will experience on its ride to the surface of the moon . This testing simulated the extreme temperatures, shaking and even the sounds that the spacecraft will experience from launch to landing. And, as JPL announced recently, the lander passed this series of tests with flying colors, as we can see in this image snapped Aug. 31 of the lander inside the 25-foot-wide (7.6 meters) space simulator at JPL. "NASA JPL’s Environmental Test Laboratory has been putting robotic explorers to the test since the Ranger program gave us NASA’s first up-close views of the moon's surface in the mid-1960s. We’re proud to provide our expertise and facilities to support this new phase of commercial lunar exploration," Charles Whetsel, manager for the Exploration Systems Development Office at JPL, said in a statement . Why is it incredible? Griffin-1 is expected to launch to the moon later this year as part of NASA's CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative. The spacecraft will carry over 1,100 pounds (455 kilograms) of cargo to its landing site near the lunar south pole. In this cargo will be science experiments and new technologies that will be tested on the moon's surface, including Astrolab's FLIP rover , which will explore the lunar surface with a history-making supercomputer onboard. This suite of experimental hardware won't just expand our understanding of the moon up close. Griffin-1's exploration will also help set the stage for a future, crewed moon base , which NASA aims to build near the south pole over the next half-decade or so.

item.title: Yemi Alade Is Counting Cash and Serving Looks in “Alhaja” Video
item.description: Yemi Alade wears a gold-embroidered black abaya in her “Alhaja” music video. We love how Yemi Alade gives us something new to talk about with each music video. If she isn’t channelling a photographer who could give Don Jazzy a run for his money, she’s stepping into the shoes of an Alhaja who clearly has money to spend, and she’s having a great time doing it. With “Alhaja”, Yemi Alade gives us another music video with a distinct visual world, memorable styling and plenty of personality. And really, would we expect anything less? item.title: What is The Hidden Cost of Nigerian Women’s Unpaid Labour?
item.description: Mother and children preparing food in a bright, cosy kitchen setting. Credit: RDNE Stock Project/Pexels. Fadekemi was six when she first felt the sting of splattered hot oil on her skin. She recalls her mother’s stern voice instructing her on how to make stew the way her father liked it. Fifty-one years and thousands of stew pots later, Fadekemi still wonders if that’s all she was made to do. In different parts of Nigeria today, there are millions of women like Fadekemi, each spending at least 5 hours daily on unpaid care and domestic work. Although Nigerians rarely pay women for care and domestic duties, research shows that it is real work with an annual economic value of up to $111 billion . How Women Carry Nigeria’s Unpaid Labour According to the Nigeria Time Use Survey (NTUS) 2024 report, the average Nigerian woman spends 21% of her day on unpaid domestic and care work ; this equals 5 extra hours, while men spend just one hour on unpaid work. This means that after spending 8 hours at work, she spends another 5 hours doing childcare and household work, making it a double shift. Yet when you look at the economic drivers of Nigeria’s economy, her time or work does not count; it is seen as a woman’s work. This inequality is seen as invisible labour. We see it show up in different phases of women’s lives, yet we still miss how heavy an unequal burden this is. Right from when a girl is 13, she becomes an unpaid labourer, doing domestic chores, taking care of siblings, yet these contributions are seen as nothing to Nigeria’s GDP. For Fadekemi, this unpaid labour started at six, continued into her teenage years, where she became a caregiver for her siblings, extended into motherhood, and now, as a grandmother, she continues to be a caregiver for her grandchildren because even traditions like Omugwo exclude men from care duties. Behind those hours of unpaid labour is a missed opportunity for the country’s GDP growth. What Happens When Care Is Shared? In a 2026 study published in BMC Paediatrics, over 64% of women said they were the primary caregivers of their newborn children. In some cases, this is a result of traditional belief systems that reinforce gender roles and assign domestic duties to women. In other cases, it is a systemic failure caused by policies that reinforce gender inequality. In Nigeria, for example, mothers are entitled to maternity leave with 50% pay, while only fathers in the civil service are entitled to 14 days of paternity leave. So what happens to private sector fathers? The national policy designs them to be absent fathers from day one and reinforces the narrative that their sole role is to be a provider and presence doesn’t matter. Experts have highlighted that cutting a new mother’s salary by 50% while excluding most fathers from paid leave reinforces the belief that a man’s primary duty is to be a financial provider and makes it harder for them to be present. And when that happens, care once again becomes the woman’s job.

item.title: 'Stupendously large black holes' aren't a major component of dark matter, study finds
item.description: null Black holes more massive than entire galaxies are not a major component of the mysterious dark matter that's thought to make up most of the matter in the cosmos, a new study finds. For decades, to explain why galaxies do not spin apart at the speeds at which they whirl, scientists have suggested the existence of an unseen substance known as dark matter , whose gravitational pull helps keep galaxies together. Dark matter is thought to make up about five-sixths of all matter in the universe . Much remains unknown about dark matter, however — including whether or not it actually exists. Black holes make good potential contenders for dark matter, since they are extremely massive and are difficult to spot in the dark depths of space. In the new study, researchers investigated whether dark matter could be made of " stupendously large black holes ," ones with masses greater than 100 billion times the mass of the sun . Stupendously large black holes greater than 1 million billion to 10 million billion suns in mass would be heavier than entire galaxies. So far, astronomers have not detected any stupendously large black holes — currently, the largest black hole known may weigh about 36 billion suns . Since researchers have not seen any even after looking at many galaxies, the new study noted they cannot make up all of dark matter — but team members wondered if the exotic objects still might constitute a significant portion of the puzzling substance. Often, dark matter is thought of "as a fine dust spread everywhere," study co-author Christopher Gerlach, a theoretical physicist at the Mainz Institute for Theoretical Physics in Germany, told Space.com. However, if dark matter is packed into a handful of gigantic objects such as stupendously large black holes, "the universe becomes grainy on very large scales. And we can check that." Specifically, the scientists analyzed the light from the dawn of the universe, study co-author Yann Gouttenoire, a theoretical physicist at the Mainz Institute for Theoretical Physics, told Space.com. For the first 380,000 years after the Big Bang , the cosmos was filled with a hot plasma in which light was trapped. Eventually, the expansion of the universe let the cosmos cool enough for the plasma to largely dissipate and form atoms. This in turn let light shine freely, "and that light is still arriving today," Gerlach explained. "We call it the cosmic microwave background , a snapshot of the infant universe covering the whole sky." The temperature of the cosmic microwave background "varies from place to place by about one part in 100,000," study co-author Antonio Iovino, a theoretical physicist at New York University, Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, told Space.com. "That pattern tells us how matter was spread back then." An illustration of a supermassive black hole against a background of dark matter. item.title: 25 and Golden! Dede Ashiogwu Celebrates in a Gorgeous Butter-Yellow Two-Piece
item.description: Dede celebrates her 25th birthday in a draped butter yellow chiffon set. Butter yellow on melanin is already a winning combination, but Big Brother Naija Season 10 star Dede is taking it somewhere much more fabulous. Celebrating her birthday on 23 October 2026, the content creator, whose full name is Ashiogwu Precious , has gifted us a set of Renaissance-inspired portraits that could easily pass for paintings in a grand old gallery. And the outfit at the centre of it all? A custom butter-yellow two-piece that makes a very good case for giving this pretty shade a spot in your wardrobe. Dede wears a custom butter yellow gathering bandeau top and low-rise train skirt by Precious Phillips. Dede handled the creative direction herself, working with designer Precious Phillips on a gathered bandeau top and a low-rise maxi skirt that follows her figure before spilling into a floor-sweeping train. The colour is gorgeous against her skin, and that dramatic silhouette gives the look a regal, almost otherworldly quality without feeling stuck in another century. Of course, the beauty look had to keep up. Yellow feathers frame her eyes, a thick side-braided ponytail sweeps through her hair, and her glowing makeup ties everything together. Add a golden hand mirror and a moody, canvas-style backdrop, and you have birthday portraits that look as though they were dreamed up in an artist’s studio. Dede poses with a golden handheld mirror in her self-styled Renaissance birthday shoot. The best part is that you don’t need a Renaissance-inspired photoshoot to take a little inspiration from Dede. Butter yellow works beautifully in flowing chiffon, sheer mesh and other lightweight fabrics, whether you’re dressing for a birthday dinner or simply want to try something new. Gold jewellery complements the shade beautifully, while pared-back accessories give statement silhouettes and playful eye makeup room to shine. Dede complements her birthday look with soft yellow feather eye flourishes and gold leaf drop earrings. Dede may have given butter yellow the full birthday-treatment treatment, but the takeaway is simple: this shade deserves a place in your fashion rotation. Ashiogwu Precious (Dede) marks her 25th birthday in a butter yellow two-piece set by Precious Phillips. Ashiogwu Precious (Dede) seated beside warm floral accents in her custom Precious Phillips birthday outfit. *** Photo Credit: Ashiogwu Precious/Instagram The post 25 and Golden!
